newsitem.title: CHINA: China tightens supervision of securities market.
newsitem.headline: China tightens supervision of securities market.

text.p: China has taken a series of steps to improve supervision on its A share markets and pre-empt possible scandals as trading hovers at record levels, analysts said on Tuesday.

The China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), the nation's top securities watchdog, has set limits on trading by stockbrokers on their own account, re-affirmed a ban on credit trading by securities houses and brokerages and decided to assign CSRC supervisors to exchanges, they said.

The central People's Bank of China has ordered all banks, futures brokerages, insurance firms and other firms except those run by securities houses and brokerages to move out of stock trading business by the year-end.
"This year, Beijing gave a green light to a quick market expansion," said one trader with a major Chinese brokerage.

"As a result, (domestic) A share and treasury bill trading have entered their most active period (in the six years of China's modern securities market), making improved supervision more necessary than before," he said.
"There are still many cases of irregularities on the markets," said one stock analyst. "This is why many wealthy investors regard recent regulations as 'negative news'."
"With market expansion peaking this year, Beijing is afraid that small loopholes could become the triggers of major scandals and is taking precautions," he added.
After years of calling its securities markets an experiment, Beijing officials this year have stressed that the market has no major problems and should continue to develop.

This has led to an unprecedented wave of share issues and listings in which around 140 companies have made their debut this year on the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses, compared with 110 for the whole of the previous peak year in 1994.
Shanghai's domestic A share index has surged more than 100 percent this year and its Shenzhen counterpart over 200 percent.
Combined average daily turnover of the two bourses has reached a record of around 20 billion yuan ($2.41 billion) in the past few weeks.
At the same time, the treasury bond market has grown extremely active. Demand for new issues appears strong and volumes on the secondary market often flirt with records.
"In the run-up to Hong Kong's takeover next year, the trend is unlikely to change," said another stock analyst. "The authorities want Shanghai and Shenzhen to be more competitive after the takeover."

In regulations published on Saturday, the CSRC said stocks held by a brokerage must not exceed 80 percent of their net assets or capital used for stock trading, based on the prices at which they bought the stocks.

A brokerage must put aside five percent of its profits from stock trading into a risk fund until the fund reaches five percent of net assets or working capital used for stock trading and then maintain that level, the regulations said.
